name: sqlite_freespace
description: Text fragments from the free space of a SQLite database's MAIN file: freelist pages, the unallocated gap of each b-tree page and the freeblock chain of freed cells. A fragment is text, not a row: no column, no table, no time, no row boundary, and the page may have belonged to something else. SENSITIVE: free pages of a messenger database hold message text and sometimes credentials, so the answer carries where each fragment is (finding_id, page, kind of region, byte offset, length in bytes and characters, encoding) and never its text; the text is written only on write_values: true, in a job run with secret_output: true, to $OUT/sqlite-freespace-values.jsonl (mode 0600, created before the scan, refused if it exists; the request is refused outside a job). Every offset is the byte position in the file and was read back from the file and compared before it was reported (offset_verified). Encodings: UTF-8 (any language) and UTF-16LE (Latin including Latin Additional, Greek including Greek Extended, Cyrillic, Armenian, Georgian, Hebrew, Arabic, Devanagari, Thai and common punctuation; CJK, kana, Hangul and emoji only in runs of at least 8 characters, a lower-confidence reading; other scripts are not found), read at either byte parity, and UTF-16BE instead of UTF-16LE where the header declares UTF-16BE; text in another encoding, in a binary column or compressed or encrypted is not found, so a negative covers only those encodings and only the regions counted under scanned. A -wal, -shm or -journal beside the file is listed with its size and NOT examined: committed changes that only the WAL holds are absent, and a rollback journal's page images are not read; a -wal or -journal that holds bytes makes the status partial. The header is validated (page size, usable size, format versions, declared size against the file); the freelist is walked with a cycle check and compared with the header's count; every freeblock chain is checked for order, bounds and loops; lock-byte and pointer-map pages are skipped and counted. Every other page is accounted for: the b-trees are walked from the roots sqlite_master lists (interior pages only; the leaves are marked), a page that is not a b-tree page is live content only when a cell of a b-tree so reached names it as an overflow page (counted under scanned.overflow_pages), and a page that no structure owns (not on the freelist the header leads to, not reached by a b-tree, not named as overflow: what a header with its freelist fields zeroed leaves, since the freed pages are no longer listed, or a table whose parent is gone) is read as free space as a listed free page is, reported as 'page in no structure', counted under scanned.pages_in_no_structure and said under problems (pages in no structure), and the status is corrupt. status is complete (every page accounted for as above, nothing inconsistent, no companion left unread), partial (a time limit, a companion not read, pages not examined, a schema that could not be read to tell which pages the b-trees own) or corrupt (the structure disagreed with itself where problems says; fragments found are still reported). Beside a -wal or -journal that holds bytes, pages that no structure owns are reported but do not make the status corrupt: the main file is then a state between two checkpoints, and the status is partial for the companion already. A file that is not SQLite is refused with its size and, if it has 256 bytes or more, the entropy of its first 4 KiB, never its first bytes. contains marks the rows of the sealed values file and nothing else: it needs write_values: true in a job run with secret_output: true (otherwise it is refused before anything is scanned). The values file has a row for EVERY fragment found, whatever the expression says, and each row carries match: 1 (the expression matched, or none was given), 0 (it did not) or 2 (it could not be decided in time); filter on match when you read the file. The file is then the same size whatever the expression is, and every row carries a random run id, so its digest differs in every run: the harness shows a job's output size and digest to whoever asked, and a file that was shorter when the expression matched less would answer, a prefix at a time, whether text you cannot see matches. The answer lists every fragment whatever the expression matched and does not say how many matched, for the same reason. What still follows the hidden text is the file's size as JSON writes it (a quote, a backslash, a control or non-ASCII character is escaped), which no expression changes. contains runs on text nobody can see, so how long it takes should not tell anything about that text either: only an expression of bounded cost is accepted (literals, classes, anchors, groups, alternation, and repeats with an upper bound of one piece that holds no choice; no *, + or {m,}, no nested repeat, no lookahead or lookbehind, no back reference, at most 256 characters, at most 256 in worst-case steps). The bound makes the difference per character small and not zero, and it adds up with the volume of hidden text: an expression of one class repeated 250 times took at most 0.06 s of CPU more on 32,768 characters of text of that class than on text of another (the slowest of the 171 accepted among 450 candidates tried; with the bound at 16384 it was 1.1 s), which is 1.4 s against 0.16 s of CPU on 22 fragments of 60,000 characters (1.3 MB) of digits against the same volume of letters, and more at the tens of megabytes an evidence disk can hold, up to the time the work budget takes (about 7 s of CPU, 10.5 s measured on a loaded machine). So the duration of the job, which whoever asked for it can see, can say that much of the free space is of a class of characters the expression matches. The answer does not: contains has a work budget in sizes the answer shows (a step is one character of a fragment times the expression's cost bound, and 1,000 for every fragment the expression is called on, whatever its length: calling it costs time on a fragment of three characters too; at most 1,000,000,000 steps and fewer for a short max_seconds), a fragment that would take the run past it is marked 2 in the values file, counted under scanned.contains_not_decided and problems, and makes the status partial, the same for any text of those sizes; and the clock of max_seconds does not run while the expression does, so status, pages_not_reached and contains_not_decided do not depend on how long it took; it skips 12 seconds at most in all (the work budget keeps it under that on a machine as fast as measured, and the limit holds where it is not), so a run with contains ends at max_seconds plus at most 12 seconds plus the time to write the answer, inside the timeout of 300 seconds. (A fragment on which the expression takes 2 seconds, which only a starved machine can cause, is marked 2 the same way.) A job whose arguments include write_values is run as secret output (the manifest declares it), and the tool refuses write_values in a job that is not. Whole results are kept: the inline page is limit rows and the rest is in the file the answer names. WHAT A REQUESTING AGENT CAN SEE. The answer, and the job's file list with each file's size and digest, are what a requester is shown without asking. The values file is sealed under store/ of the sandbox, which an agent's VM mounts read-only: an agent that opens it reads every row, the values (and match) included. The measures above protect what is shown without anyone opening the file (the answer, its status and counts, the size and digest); they do not stop an agent that deliberately opens the sealed file, and this tool does not decide whether it may (that is the sandbox's mounts). Not a deleted-record reconstruction, not a WAL or journal reader, and not a statement that a database was or was not vacuumed.

db.description: A SQLite database file (the main file; its -wal and -journal are listed, not read)

min_length.description: Shortest run of text, in characters (default 6, at least 3)

contains.description: Case-insensitive regex over a fragment's text; it sets match on the rows of the values file (1 matched, 0 did not, 2 not decided in time) and drops none: every fragment is a row, and the answer lists all of them and does not say which matched. Needs write_values: true, in a job run with secret_output: true. Only an expression of bounded cost is accepted: at most 256 characters, repeats only with an upper bound ({m,n} or ?, not *, + or {m,}) and only of a piece that holds no choice, no lookahead, lookbehind or back reference, and a worst case of at most 256 steps. Its time does not count toward max_seconds, up to 12 seconds in all; it has a work budget (a character of a fragment times the expression's cost bound, and 1,000 for every fragment it is called on, at most 1,000,000,000 steps): a fragment past it is marked 2 and the status is partial, the same for any text of those sizes. How long the job takes can still follow the hidden text

limit.description: Fragments in the inline answer (default 200, and at most 1 MiB of rows); the whole list is in the file the answer names

write_values.description: Write each fragment's text to $OUT/sqlite-freespace-values.jsonl, one row per fragment found, with match and a per-run run id (default false). Refused unless the tool runs as a job, which must be run with secret_output: true; the answer never carries a text

max_seconds.description: Stop before the next page after this long (default 240, at most 270); the time contains takes does not count, up to 12 seconds in all (it has its own work budget, lower for a short max_seconds); the pages not reached are counted and the answer says partial
